runs.t: Red Hat Enterprise Linux System Administration I

is a written record of events on a system. This chapter shows you where Linux keeps its logs, how to read them to find problems, how to keep them after a reboot, and how to keep the clock correct so the time stamps in logs can be trusted.
Programs and the kernel write down events, and these records help you audit the system and fix problems.

is the core of the operating system. Together with other programs, it keeps a diary of what happens: who logged in, what failed, what started. Think of a ship's logbook. The comparison stops here: a ship's captain writes by hand, while Linux writes automatically.

Correct time on every machine is critical when you compare logs from several systems.

(Network Time Protocol) is the standard way for machines to get the correct time from the Internet. A machine can use public NTP services such as the NTP Pool Project, or a good local hardware clock. It is like checking your watch against the station clock.
Run as any user. It only reads.
A time zone name tells the system how to turn UTC into local time.

. Choosing the right name can be tricky: much of Arizona does not use daylight saving time, so it uses
asks you questions about your location and prints the correct name. It changes nothing.
